# How an answer is drawn

<!-- Generated by web/scripts/design-brief.ts from the web app's own types. Do not
     edit: the fields, their order and the rule on each come from the source, and
     web/src/ui/brief.test.ts fails if this file and the types disagree. -->

You never write markup, a colour, a glyph or a position. You write one JSON answer and
the app renders it with the design it owns. What is yours: which nodes the question asks
for, how many items it holds, the order they read in, the composition, and what
each item opens when a reader clicks it. Fill every shape below with real records —
an item whose provenance you cannot name is an item you have not written yet.

## The order to think in

Written here rather than derived from a type: no TypeScript union says in what order to
reason, and an answer written in one leap comes out as a paragraph, because a paragraph
is the shortest thing that finishes a sentence. Five passes, in this order.

1. **Read the question.** Name what would settle it — a quantity, a comparison, a
   mechanism, a location in a file, a chain of who-said-what, a decision. One noun, not
   a sentence; everything after this follows it.
2. **Read the graph around it, before you plan anything.** Pull the records that answer
   it AND what is wired to them: which claim this one supports, which run produced it,
   which experiment refutes it, which prior it answers. Two facts get decided here and
   nowhere else — what the answer may claim (a record you did not open is a record you
   cannot cite), and which parts belong together (a wire between two records is why they
   share a `card`, or a tier of the same `flow`, instead of two unrelated sections). You
   assert no edge; the store holds them. Reading them is what makes this a graph answer
   rather than a search result.
3. **Plan the canvas, then fill it.** The layout that is yours is the reading order and
   the grouping — ink, position and size are the app's. Decide what reads first, which
   items sit in one container, which share a `row` (lead / fill / trail), which belong
   across a `tier` of `card`s, a `flow` you wire, or the `graph` the store wires; and
   where prose keeps the reading measure, not the full span. Say the plan back as one
   line per part: part · node · how many · what it opens when clicked.
4. **Design each part separately, against its own rule.** Each line of that plan is a
   decision made from the arm's own `*When:*` rule below and from nothing else. This file
   maps no subject onto a node: a mapping here is a lookup an answer performs instead of
   a judgement it makes, and two answers handed the same lookup and the same records come
   out the same page. The arms carry the distinctions where each node is registered.
   Most answers hold several kinds; a surface using one node for all of them has thrown
   away the parts that were not prose. Count what the records hold before dressing it and
   write that count into `budget`: the app counts the render and checks it, and a guessed
   number is the one part no later step can repair.
5. **Render it once, as one answer.** The order is yours and this file gives none. What
   decides it is the question: a reader's first glance should land on whatever carries
   this answer's weight — a quantity, a disagreement, a mechanism, a queue, an address —
   and step 2 is where you learned which. An order stated here is the quickest way to
   make every answer the same page. The opening item is the author's as well: a page may
   open on a `drawing`, a `figure`, a `graph`, a `tier` or an `embed` when one of those
   carries the weight, and nothing requires it to open on a heading and prose. A `heading` per part a reader would name, nothing
   under a heading that does not belong to it. Then check what a first pass gets wrong:
   is every number and name here on the records, and is any node here only because the
   lane looked empty? A node you cannot cite is deleted, not reworded.

No one-size-fits-all blueprint is offered: a question about a knowledge cluster
does not want the same opening, grouping or density as a question about a
measurement. The sequence — the leading node, the grouping, the density,
the depth of a card — is derived fresh for every answer from the records in
step 2, and the derivation must be re-checkable from those records. A
composition that recurs across unrelated answers with only nouns swapped
is a template, not a decision the answer made.
The surface is the answer's own compromise. A parts list is resolved by
the reader's eye, so the plan in step 3 is kept to the parts themselves,
one node per weight, the order the weight gives the first glance, and the
top-level budget. It is never a template for the next answer.
**No sequence is selected for you**: do not assume a heading-then-prose-then-figure-then-table-then-visual order. Derive the opening item, grouping, and density from the answer's weight in step 2 for every surface. A repeated first → second → third pattern across answers is a hardcoded design, not an authored composition.
Never use a tier of two cards for competing hypotheses; use flow/graph/drawing/figure for the mechanism.
**Pre-display verification gate**: before publishing, render live, screenshot full height, run verify-canvas.ts + manual review for lines crossing labels, box overlaps, clipping, zero-size elements, refused nodes, on-palette ink. Fix defects or name them explicitly — never display a known-broken surface.
**The steps cost reasoning, not calls.** One read of the graph, one write of the flow,
one publish. A surface that arrives late is not one that thought too little; it is one
that round-tripped. So do not re-fetch what is already in hand, do not draw half the
answer and then go looking for the rest, and do not publish twice: by the time you write
the JSON, steps 1 to 4 are finished and the only thing left is typing it.

## What exists to build with

- `Prose` · ui/sections.tsx — A paragraph at answer size, with its `backticked` tokens read as code. *When:* Two to four sentences of what the records say, at answer size, backticked tokens as code. A number, a list or a mechanism has a more specific node — prose is what none of them holds.
- `Marks` · ui/sections.tsx — Lines each carrying a glyph: `+` kept, `−` broken, `·` neutral, `→` the one demand. *When:* A list. Prose never holds one — a list inside a paragraph is a list the design cannot put a glyph on, and the glyph is the verdict.
- `Section` · ui/sections.tsx — A section rule: the label, the hairline carrying the width, the measure at its end. *When:* A rule over a group of nodes: the label names the group, the hairline carries its width, and a measure sits at its end in the machine register. What that measure states — a size, a span, a count — is yours to pick for what the group actually holds.
- `Table` · ui/table.tsx — A table as its source prints it: the caption whole, the columns in its order. *When:* Figures a source already laid out in a grid. Quote it; never re-shape it, and never re-order its columns. *Composition:* the caption, the columns in the source's order, one array per row with the row's own name first
- `Chart` · vega-lite + vega-embed — A figure from the answer's own rows, in the design's ink. *When:* Rows you are comparing — a count per kind, a spread across arms. The spec carries data, marks and encoding; a spec that names a colour, a font, a title or a config is refused, because on this surface a hue is a verdict.
- `Series` · uPlot — A metric curve over steps, on a canvas. *When:* An Experiment's metric series — thousands of ordered points. Two or three curves on one x. A curve on its own steps is a second Series, never a second line here.
- `Equation` · KaTeX — A formula as its source writes it, in TeX. *When:* A formula a paper or a record states. Display is the only block form. A formula that will not parse prints as its own source in machine ink — never as an error, and never dropped.
- `Register` · @tanstack/react-virtual — A strip or a list longer than its lane, mounted a window at a time. *When:* Any run of items that can exceed the pane — a replay of commits, a register of shapes. It scrolls on its own axis; it never wraps to a second row and never drops its tail. *Composition:* the axis (`x` a strip, `y` a list), the item count, and one item's extent
- `Paths` · ui/sections.tsx — Addresses under a sentence about them, two to a row, in machine ink. *When:* The files a finding sits on. Each ends at the line it is about. Print them whole — a reader pastes one into a shell.
- `Prose/Markdown` · react-markdown + remark-gfm — Stored markdown as the record holds it. *When:* Text the store already carries — a record's description, a paper's abstract. Read, never written.
- `Rich` · @tiptap/react — The one surface that is written into rather than read. *When:* Text a person is composing. Not for anything the store already holds — that is Prose/Markdown, which costs no editor.
- `Flow` · ui/flow.tsx (React Flow) — Agent-authored knowledge flow: carded blocks in tiers with named, arrowed relations (supports, came from, narrows). *When:* When the answer is how one thing came from another — what formed a claim, what a change broke, how a result was arrived at. The relation is the finding. Pick this over `graph` when the reading is yours. *Composition:* blocks with slot/tier, relations with label, optional height
- `Graph` · ui/compose.tsx (React Flow KnowledgeGraph) — Store territory: every record within hops of the focal record, drawn as the fold with labelled wires. *When:* When the weight is in the relations the store already holds. Pick this over `flow` when the territory is the store's and the reader is doing the reading.
- `Figure` · ui/figure.tsx (Vega-Lite + uPlot + KaTeX + NumTable) — A figure an answer places: chart, series, equation, or NumTable figure. *When:* Rows you are comparing, a metric curve over steps, a formula a paper states, or a table a source printed. The spec carries data, marks and encoding; a value the code does not produce is never drawn.
- `Text` · ui/compose.tsx (register lines) — A line of text at one of the surface's three registers. *When:* `chrome` is the 10.5px uppercase mono for labels and locations; `machine` is a value read off an instrument, white, in the machine face; `read` is the paragraph a surface is read for.
- `Plotly` · plotly.js — Interactive scientific figure (scatter, heatmap, treemap, sunburst, embedding, 3D). *When:* When the scientist needs zoom/pan/hover, 40+ Plotly chart types, UMAP/t-SNE scatter colored by cluster, or a 3D scene. Vega-Lite is the static fallback; Plotly is the interactive one.
- `LearningCurve` · uPlot — Multi-arm learning curve over steps, with hover crosshair. *When:* When comparing training runs over steps — loss, accuracy, reward. Two or three curves on one x. Not a table.
- `Confusion` · Vega-Lite (rect + text) — Confusion matrix, ROC, and PR curves as first-class figures. *When:* Classification evaluation where the matrix or the curve is the verdict. A confusion matrix heatmap with counts, ROC with AUC, PR with average precision.
- `Embedding` · Plotly (scatter) — UMAP / t-SNE / PCA embedding scatter colored by cluster or label, with hover identity. *When:* High-dimensional records projected to 2D. Points are records; color is cluster/label; hover names the point. Vega-Lite needs a transform; Plotly carries it.
- `MermaidMindmap` · mermaid — Mermaid mind map and flowchart diagram from markdown-like text definitions. *When:* When the answer is a hierarchy or a causal chain that reads better as a mind map than as text. Mermaid renders the definition; the app owns ink.
- `Markmap` · markmap-lib — Interactive mind map rendered from Markdown (markmap). *When:* When the answer is a hierarchy that can be authored in Markdown and rendered interactively. The mind map is the presentation, Markdown is the source.
- `Choropleth` · Plotly (choropleth) — Geospatial choropleth for studies/trials by region or site. *When:* When the finding is spatial: per-region rates, site-level outcomes, or geographic spread. Plotly carries it; Vega-Lite does not geo-project.
- `Sankey` · Plotly / Vega-Lite (sankey) — Sankey flow diagram for proportional movement between stages. *When:* When value moves between states — budget to options to cost, tokens to clusters, or cohort attrition. The width is the quantity.
- `Network` · React Flow (Gephi-lite) — Read-only network graph with centrality and community as position. *When:* When the answer is about a data/attention network, not the formation graph. Position is centrality; color is community; the layout is derived, not authored.

## The figure menu: the mark follows the shape

A figure kind is chosen by the shape of the rows, never by the previous answer's habit:
three answers drawing `series` with different nouns are one template, and a reader
feels that before they can name it. Before placing a `figure`, name the shape of the
data, take the mark from this menu, and when two kinds would both carry it, say in the
label why the loser lost. The app owns ink, so variety cannot come from colour: two
surfaces differing only in palette are one surface drawn twice. The type is yours.

- One quantity over a genuinely continuous span → `series` (line): the line asserts
  interpolation between points, so the span must really be continuous.
- A few arms compared at separate points → `chart` bars or dot plot: no line through
  0.3, 1.2 and 5 ns, nothing exists at 0.4.
- The story is the delta between two arms → bars of the difference, or a slope chart.
- A winner plus its margin per row → `table` with the margin beside it; bars only when
  the ranking is itself the reading.
- Density or value over a 2D field → `chart` rect marks, or a Plotly heatmap.
- Part-to-whole, or movement between stages → Sankey or a stacked area.
- Many categories over one period → recharts radar or bar; a share of a whole → pie.
- Points in high dimensions, named by cluster → `embedding`.
- Training runs over steps → `learningcurve`; classification verdicts → `confusion`.
- Surfaces, volumes, anything a reader orbits → Plotly 3D.
- A mechanism that runs, or an evolution no frozen frame holds → `drawing` with SMIL,
  or a published `embed`.
- Records and their wires → `graph`, which is not a chart at all.

## ComposedFlow
A composed answer: the question, and the items that answer it.
- `title` · string
- `prompt` · string
- `budget?` · Record<string, number> — The answer's own ceiling, set before it is composed: how many of each node may draw, keyed by the node names used. Counted off the render and checked, not trusted — LAW.md's noise budget says what it is for.
- `compose` · readonly Item[] — The items, in the order they read. This is the composition — there is no second grammar, because a composed surface reads down the page.

## Item
One item of a composition: a catalog node, and what that node holds.
Each arm is written with `node` set to its name below.
- `heading` · { level: "1" | "2" | "3", text: string } — A document heading at one of three ranks. The node for an answer that reads as a document: one `1`, a `2` per part, a `3` per point. Pick this over `section` whenever the surface is prose rather than telemetry — a page of section rules has no hierarchy a reader can see.
- `section` · { label: string, size?: string } — A section rule: a label, the hairline carrying the width, and the measure at its end, in the machine register. The node for a measurement pane — a sampled run, a register of shapes — where the measure at the end is the point.
- `prose` · { text: string, lead?: boolean, span?: boolean } — Prose. Two to four sentences; `backticked` tokens read as code. Measured at ~75 characters by default (the app's figure, not yours). Set `span` for a lead under full-width chrome — a narrow paragraph under a wide header reads as unfinished.
- `cells` · { cells: readonly string[] } — A machine line: cells read for their figures, in the machine face, spaced into a column by the first one. The node for a measurement whose parts are all figures — never `prose`, which sets a number in the prose face. When the row needs a gutter at its right, or a label in a different register from its values, compose a `row` instead: this is the shorthand for the common case.
- `marks` · { items: readonly Mark[], span?: boolean } — Marked lines. The glyph is the verdict and the only coloured thing.
- `paths` · { items: readonly string[] } — Addresses under a sentence about them, two to a row.
- `footnote` · { text: string } — The prior, the one line out of somebody else's ledger.
- `figure` · { figure: Figure } — A figure: a chart, a series, a table, an equation.
- `code` · Code — A file on stage, highlighted and numbered, with annotations pinned to their own line. Never `prose` — no gutter, no line numbers.
- `image` · ImageItem — A real figure, fetched, never drawn or guessed. Not Rich — this is display, not composing text; Rich costs an editor you do not need to show one picture.
- `illustration` · IllustrationItem — A video that dramatizes a mechanism, with the prompt that made it printed on the surface. Pick this when what a reader must see is what something LOOKS like rather than what it reaches — a number belongs in `figure`, and this node is labelled illustrative precisely so a video never reads as a measurement.
- `drawing` · Drawing — Geometry the agent drew itself, when no catalog shape is the right shape, and the shape for a simple directly labelled value: hand-write the marks at coordinates taken from the records' own numbers, and name every axis and unit inside the SVG. Reach for a library node (`figure`, `series`) only when its scales, legends or real sampling materially improve the result — never to decorate a number that reads in one line.
- `embed` · { id: string, title: string, shows: string, height?: number } — A page you wrote and published, hosted live in the answer: the shape of a thing, a running simulation, anything whose geometry this catalog does not hold — and nothing else. The host grants no new permission, so the page inherits no ink and can fetch nothing. `shows` says what it shows — a hosted page nobody can describe is a black box — and `height` is the lane it draws in. `A page you write yourself`, below, carries the contract: what the sandbox forbids, the inks to copy, what a first draft must get right.
- `plate` · { bar: string, title?: string, byline?: string, items: readonly Item[] } — A quoted page: the address it was opened at, an optional centred title/byline, then any items — a `prose` quote, a `figure` table, an `image` — all re-themed to the page's own light colours, because a printed paper does not take the reader's dark mode. Pick this to hold anything reproduced FROM a source rather than written about it; nest the source's own table inside it rather than beside it, so a reader sees the page and not a description of the page.
- `card` · { items: readonly Item[], lane?: number, slot?: string } — A bordered container holding a composition of its own: a knowledge block, a commit in a replay, a quoted plate. General, not a template — the box is a hairline and a step of surface, and what goes in it is whatever you compose. `lane` is its width in `ch` when a tier of them must come out even.
- `tier` · { items: readonly Item[] } — A tier: cards or items laid across the lane, centred, wrapping when they exceed it. The geometry a flow of blocks hangs in — one up, three down is two tiers.
- `flow` · { blocks: readonly { readonly slot: string; readonly tier: number; readonly items: readonly Item[] }[], relations: readonly { readonly from: string; readonly to: string; readonly label: string; readonly open?: boolean }[], height?: number } — A flow: carded blocks in tiers and the relations between them, routed by React Flow. The statement an ordered list of sections cannot make is "THIS block belongs to THAT one, in this word", so a relation is named here rather than laid out. You give each block a tier and each relation its own word; the routing, the arrowhead and the pan are the library's, and the ink is the theme's.
- `rule` — A hairline. Opens or closes a set of rows; the only rule the agent may place, because a rule is structure and not decoration.
- `row` · { lead?: readonly Item[], fill?: readonly Item[], trail?: readonly Item[], lead_ch?: number, trail_ch?: number, pitch?: "tight" | "open" } — A row with up to three slots: `lead` keeps its width and is what the column is scanned by, `fill` takes the rest, `trail` is a gutter at the far right that aligns down the surface. This is the geometry behind a label/values/marker row and behind a head with its actions on the right — one node, not two templates. It is also the ranked list: a `section` over N of these, ordered by what each would settle — the lead is what the reader scans to choose, the fill the claim, the trail what it costs. There is no leaderboard node to ask for because this is it.
  - `lead_ch?` · number — The lead's width in `ch`, when a column of rows must align on one.
  - `trail_ch?` · number — The trail's width in `ch`, so every gutter mark meets the same edge.
  - `pitch?` · "tight" | "open" — Pitch: `tight` for a scanned column, `open` for a sampled run that is read down. A run of rows at prose leading becomes a block of digits.
- `text` · { register: "chrome" | "machine" | "read", text: string, span?: boolean } — A line of text at one of the surface's three registers. `chrome` is the 10.5px uppercase mono that labels and locates; `machine` is a value read off an instrument, white, in the machine face; `read` is the one paragraph a surface is read for, at reading size. Pick `chrome` for anything that is not itself an answer.
  - `span?` · boolean — Whether the block takes the whole lane instead of the reading measure. A paragraph is measured by default, because ~75 characters is where a reader starts losing the line coming back from the right edge — that figure is the app's and not yours. Whether this block is a column someone reads or a band across the pane IS yours: set it when the block is a banner, a summary line under a full-width run, or anything whose job is to span what it describes.
- `chip` · { text: string, on?: boolean } — A chip: a boxed mono control — a lens offering another reading, a filter. `on` is the one already open.
- `field` · { placeholder: string, can?: string } — A line to type into, so a surface ends in a question rather than a full stop. `can` states what it could still be asked.
- `register` · { axis: "x" | "y", extent: number, gap?: number, label: string, rows: readonly (readonly Item[])[], height?: number } — A strip or a list longer than its lane. It scrolls on its own axis and never drops its tail — which is the whole reason a long run of rows is this and not a repeated `marks`. Each row is itself a composition, so a sampled row can carry its own marks.
  - `height?` · number — The strip's own height, required on `axis: "x"` — a horizontal register's items are positioned absolutely, so nothing else gives the lane a height and it draws nothing without one. A card of two or three lines needs ~220–280.
- `graph` · { record: string, hops?: "1" | "2" | "3", open?: string, height?: number } — The knowledge graph, opened at one record and drawn as the fold: every record within `hops` as a block in a tier, and one labelled, arrowed wire per stored edge between two of them. The node for an answer whose weight is in the relations — and the only composition node whose edges are not yours: you name a record, the store says what bears on it, with the valence a `flow` relation would have to assert. Pick by whose reading the reader is doing: `flow` states YOURS, tier by tier and word by word; `graph` hands over the territory to find their own way in.
  - `record` · string — The record the window centres on, by id.
  - `hops?` · "1" | "2" | "3" — How far the window lights: 1 to 3 edges, default 2.
  - `open?` · string — A block to open the formation panel on, by record id: the claim whose own sources and wires the reader should see unfolded without clicking for it.
- `code_context` · { super_header?: string, file: string, commit?: string, feed_flow?: { input: { label: string, note: string }, relation1: string, guard: { label: string, note: string }, relation2: string, output: { label: string, note: string } }, code: { path: string, start_line: number, lit_line: number, source: string, run_groups: readonly {
          readonly label: string;
          readonly target_line: number;
          readonly chips: readonly string[];
          readonly note: string;
          readonly tag?: string;
        }[] }, callout?: string, matrix?: { label: string, grid: readonly (readonly string[])[], caption: string, finding_title: string, finding_body: string }, next_question?: { label: string, text: string, action: string } } — A file in context: upstream supply flow, syntax-highlighted code lines with pinned outcome run cards, matrix schematic, and next question exposed. Pick this over `code` when explaining how code paths route different configurations or kernels.
- `review_accordion` · { super_header?: string, title: string, subtitle?: string, meta_left?: string, meta_right?: string, items: readonly {
        readonly num: string;
        readonly title: string;
        readonly badge: string;
        readonly open?: boolean;
        readonly prose?: string;
        readonly pipeline?: readonly { readonly name: string; readonly desc: string }[];
        readonly pipeline_caption?: string;
        readonly routing_table?: readonly {
          readonly tokens: string;
          readonly before: string;
          readonly after: string;
          readonly configs: string;
        }[];
        readonly added_lines?: { readonly count: number; readonly file: string };
        readonly action_label?: string;
      }[], settlement?: { title: string, status: string, branch_a: { label: string, name: string, detail: string }, branch_b: { label: string, name: string, detail: string }, note: string, caption: string, action: string } } — A behavioral review with risk accordions: before/after routing table, pipeline stages, diff lines, and settlement proposals. Pick this over `prose` when reviewing a PR, commit, or behavioral change where code routing shifted without proving measured performance.
- `pipeline` · { steps: readonly { readonly title: string; readonly note: string }[], caption?: string } — A horizontal pipeline of transformation stages connected by arrows. Pick this over `flow` when displaying a simple sequential dataflow or configuration pass.
- `matrix_schematic` · { label: string, grid: readonly (readonly string[])[], caption: string, finding_title: string, finding_body: string } — A 2D matrix or block mask schematic showing pairwise retention vs drop. Pick this over `figure` when analyzing sparsity grids, block masks, or attention patterns.
- `settlement` · { title: string, status?: string, branch_a: { label: string, name: string, detail: string }, branch_b: { label: string, name: string, detail: string }, note: string, caption?: string, action?: string } — An experimental settlement proposal card contrasting two concrete branches. Pick this over `card` when proposing an A/B control experiment to settle an open hypothesis.

## Figure
A figure an answer places: the catalog node, and what that node needs.
Each arm is written with `kind` set to its name below.
- `chart` · Chart
- `series` · Series
- `equation` · Equation
- `table` · { table: NumTable, derive?: boolean }
- `plotly` · { data: PlotlyData, layout?: PlotlyLayout, label?: string } — Interactive scientific figure (scatter, heatmap, treemap, sunburst, embedding, 3D) for scientists who need zoom/pan/hover and 40+ Plotly chart types.
- `recharts` · { type: RechartsType, data: RechartsData, label?: string } — Rich interactive chart (Area, Bar, Line, Radar, Radial, Pie) for dense multi-axis comparison when Vega-Lite is not enough.
- `learningcurve` · { curves: Series["curves"], unit?: string, height?: number } — Multi-arm learning curve over steps with hover crosshair for comparing training runs.
- `confusion` · { matrix: readonly (readonly number[])[], labels: readonly string[], title?: string } — Confusion matrix, ROC, and PR curves as first-class evaluation figures.
- `embedding` · { points: readonly { readonly x: number; readonly y: number; readonly label: string; readonly cluster?: string }[], title?: string } — UMAP / t-SNE / PCA embedding scatter colored by cluster, with hover identity.

## RechartsType
- "area" | "bar" | "line" | "radar" | "radial" | "pie"

## Chart
A figure the answer draws from its own rows.
- `spec` · Record<string, unknown> — The Vega-Lite spec: `data.values` the rows, `mark` the form, `encoding` the fields each axis reads — your own field names, whatever the records call them. Marks, scales, axes, tooltips, layers and transforms are all available. Three keys are refused, because the theme owns them and `ChartView` rejects a spec carrying any: `config`, `background`, `title`. Nothing else is refused — in particular a hue is not, and you never need to name one for the figure to come out in the design's ink. What the figure is of goes in `label`.
- `label` · string — What the figure is of, for the reader a screen reader gives it to.

## Series
A metric series over steps.
- `curves` · readonly Curve[]
- `unit?` · string — The x axis's unit, as the record counts it: `step`.
- `height?` · number

## Curve
One curve: its name, and the value at each step.
- `key` · string — The metric as the record keys it: `grad_norm`, `loss`.
- `steps` · readonly number[] — The steps, ascending — the x of every point.
- `values` · readonly number[] — The value at each step, the same length as `steps`.

## Equation
A formula, as the paper or the record prints it.
- `tex` · string — The formula in TeX, exactly as the source writes it: `\sigma(\sum_i v_i)`.
- `display?` · boolean — Display sets it on its own line, which is the only block form; inline rides the sentence around it.

## NumTable
A table as its source prints it: the caption whole, the headers in order, one array per row with the row's own name first. A cell is a number where the source prints a figure, and the source's own text where it prints `—`.
- `caption` · string — The table's label and caption, quoted whole: `Table 1. Benchmark results …`.
- `columns` · readonly string[] — The column headers, in the source's order.
- `rows` · readonly (readonly (string | number)[])[] — One array per row: the row's own name, then one cell per column.

## Column
One column read off the drawn cells: the figures it prints, the precision it prints them at, and the spread between its own extremes.
- `name` · string
- `places` · number
- `spread` · string | "null"

## Code
A file on stage. GIVE IT THE WHOLE FILE: the card cuts an 18-line window around the first `highlight`, and its header opens the file entire, scrolling, those lines still lit. Cut `text` down yourself and "full code" reopens what was already drawn. Two regions far apart are two nodes, each with an honest `from`.
- `path` · string — The path, as its own header line: `nanochat/block_sparse.py`.
- `text` · string — The file's entire text. Not an excerpt — the node excerpts, you do not.
- `language?` · string — Empty autodetects from the extension.
- `from?` · number — The file line that `text` starts at: 1 for a whole file, which is the normal case.
- `highlight?` · readonly number[] — The lines to land on first, in file numbering. The card's window centres on the first.
- `notes?` · readonly CodeNote[]

## CodeNote
One gutter chip, pinned to the line it annotates.
- `line` · number — The 1-based line this chip annotates; floating notes are forbidden.
- `text` · string

## ImageItem
A figure as its source holds it.
- `src` · string — Where it was fetched, verbatim — never a guessed or constructed URL.
- `alt` · string — What the figure shows, for the reader a screen reader gives it.
- `caption?` · string — The source's own caption, quoted — "Figure 2: …" as the paper wrote it.

## IllustrationItem
A video a generator rendered from a prompt. Composed only when a video-generation tool is actually connected and actually returned a `src` — never a guessed or future URL, the same rule `image` holds for a fetched figure.
- `src` · string — Where it was rendered, verbatim.
- `prompt` · string — The prompt exactly as sent, printed in full — the honest gap between what was asked for and what a reader sees is theirs to judge, not smoothed over.
- `inspiredBy` · string — The real paper or figure this dramatizes. Never implies the video measures it.
- `alt` · string

## Drawing
A visual the agent drew itself.
- `body` · string — The SVG body — the agent's own marks, without the outer `<svg>` wrapper, which this node supplies so the viewBox and sizing stay the app's. A body may move: the SMIL timing elements are allowed, and this node injects the body by a route that registers them, so a sweep or a value advancing over time is something to compose.
- `viewBox` · string — The coordinate space the body draws in: `0 0 w h`. The agent picks it to suit the geometry rather than being handed a fixed stage.
- `label` · string — What it shows, for a reader given it by a screen reader. A drawing with no description is refused: an unlabelled custom visual is the one thing a reader cannot fall back to prose for.
- `height?` · number

## FlowBlock
One block in the flow: its slot, what it holds, and the tier it hangs in.
- `slot` · string — The slot the relations name it by, `K#1`.
- `tier` · number — The tier it sits in, 0 at the top. One up and three down is tiers 0 and 1.
- `body` · ReactNode — Rendered by the caller, so a block is whatever the composition put in it.

## FlowRelation
One relation, as its own word reads it.
- `from` · string
- `to` · string
- `label` · string
- `open?` · boolean — A want rather than an assertion — drawn dashed.

## KnowledgeFlow
A whole answer: the prompt that asked for it, and the flow that answers it.
- `title` · string — The answer's name, as the header reads it: `1.3B divergence · Issue#15`.
- `prompt` · string — The prompt that asked, shown as it was typed.
- `anchor?` · string — The block the flow reads from, top and centre; the most-wired one when unset.
- `rows?` · readonly (readonly string[])[] — The composition, when the distiller wants it said outright: each inner array is one row of blocks, top first — `[[K#1], [K#2, K#3, K#4]]` is one up, three down. Unset, the rows derive from the edges' distance from the anchor.
- `blocks` · readonly KnowledgeBlock[]
- `edges` · readonly FlowEdge[]
- `files?` · readonly { readonly path: string; readonly text: string; readonly language?: string }[]

## KnowledgeBlock
A block of knowledge: one distilled claim, and the records it stands on.
- `id` · string — The block's id as its card wears it, `K#1`.
- `status` · BlockStatus
- `title` · string — The claim itself, an assertion rather than a name.
- `body` · string — The claim's body, in prose; `backticks` mark its mono tokens.
- `derived` · string — What the block is, as its chip reads: `derived · 3 records`.
- `provenance` · string — The provenance footer: `3 records · Issue#15 ×2 · step 17,900`.
- `chain?` · readonly ChainRow[] — The records behind the claim, told when the card is expanded.
- `figure?` · Figure — The figure those records are a measurement of, shown with the chain when the block is opened: a `chart` of rows being compared, a `series` of a metric over steps, a `table` as its source prints it, an `equation` as it is stated. Pick the node from the catalog in LAW.md; a claim whose evidence is a number reads better as the figure than as a sentence about it.

## ChainRow
One row of a block's chain: the record that found it, what it found, and when.
- `ref` · string — The record as its ref reads, `Issue#15`; a click could open it.
- `note` · string — What that record found, as one line of prose.
- `meta` · string — Where and when it was found: `Josh · step 17,900 · grad_norm 0.8 → 41.3`.

## FlowEdge
One step of the flow: block `from`'s knowledge, as `kind` reads, into `to`. `why` is the distiller's own reason for the wire — what the modal says when a reader asks how this connection was made.
- `from` · string
- `to` · string
- `kind` · EdgeKind
- `why?` · string

## BlockStatus
How a block stands: settled by records, still open, or awaiting what has not run.
- "settled" | "open" | "awaited"

## EdgeKind
How one block's knowledge flows into another, as the edge's label reads.
- "leads to" | "leaves open" | "exposes" | "rests on" | "needs" | "awaits"

## MarkKind
What a mark says about the line beside it: kept, wrong, plain, the one demand, or — in a row's own gutter — the reading that is out of place. `flag` is the row-level one: a verdict about a measurement rather than about a sentence, which is why it takes a glyph of its own. The first line is the one demand and takes the arrow — the exact column, constant or test to write. The rest stand beside it.
- "fit" | "finding" | "note" | "demand" | "flag"

## Mark
A line with a glyph on it. The glyph is the component's choice, never the model's.
- `kind` · MarkKind
- `text` · string

## UI dynamism: proactive visual composition

An answer on this canvas is a graphical instrument, never a chat transcript or a wall of prose.
When answering a question, never default to text paragraphs or raw markdown tables. Proactively reach
for the catalog's custom components to present structure, metrics, comparisons, and mechanisms:

- **Never dump the answer into Chat.** Chat is strictly the conversation control log and executive index —
  it must hold at most one or two sentences pointing the reader to the canvas. Every table, sweep,
  quantitative comparison, hypothesis card, and knowledge graph belongs ON THE CANVAS. An agent that dumps
  markdown tables, detailed numerical sweeps, and lists into Chat while leaving the Canvas sparse has
  completely inverted the product.
- **Metrics and sweeps go in `figure` tables, never text or chat.** Tabular figures, benchmark results,
  hyperparameter sweeps, ablation runs, turnover numbers, and performance metrics MUST use `figure` with `kind: "table"`
  and a `NumTable` payload (`caption`, `columns`, `rows`). Never print markdown tables in Chat or monospace ASCII grids.
  The app automatically measures column widths, formats decimal precision, and renders derived spreads.
- **Competing hypotheses and alternatives sit in a `tier` of `card`s.** When comparing multiple leads,
  branches, models, or candidate explanations, do not describe them sequentially in prose. Group them side-by-side
  across a `tier` of `card`s with `lane` set (e.g. `36`–`45ch`). Each card holds its own composition —
  headings, prose, metrics, and marks — allowing the reader to compare branches at a glance.
- **Knowledge, claims, and relations proactively embed `graph` within the canvas.** When an answer touches
  beliefs, issues, experiments, or causal formation wires, PROACTIVELY include a `graph` node naming the focal record
  (`{ node: "graph", record: UUID, hops: 2 }`). Do not wait for the user to ask for the graph, and never isolate
  it onto a separate full page: embedding it renders the interactive React Flow knowledge canvas with claim cards,
  evidence badges, and formation lines directly inside the canvas stream alongside the other blocks.
  The `graph` node auto-populates each block's title and description from the store — you do not author them.
- **When YOU want to author the graph content, use `flow` instead of `graph`.** `flow` is the agent-authored
  knowledge graph: you compose each block explicitly with items of your own writing. Use `flow` when the answer
  demands analytical narrative per node — a causal explanation, a mechanism summary, a method description —
  rather than a raw store readout. In a `flow`, every block MUST carry the full anatomy below; a bare-title
  node is an empty shell that deprives the reader of context and is never acceptable.
- **Knowledge graph node anatomy: title, short description, slot, and provenance.** Every block in a `flow`
  MUST carry full substantive anatomy, never just a bare title:
  1. **Slot badge (`K#1`, `K#2`, ...)**: Machine address identifying the block's reading rank in the fold.
  2. **Title (heading or bold prose)**: Prominent 1–3 line headline stating the belief, question, method, or finding.
  3. **Short description (prose item, 2–4 lines)**: Concrete technical substance the AI authors from the records —
     empirical metrics, sample windows, mechanism specifics, ablation findings, or method steps.
     A node without a short description is an empty shell that fails the reader.
  4. **Provenance footer (chrome text)**: Record kind, sequence number, and evidence count.
  5. **Labeled orthogonal wires**: Every wire between nodes carries an explicit relational verb (`supports`,
     `came from`, `rests on`, `narrows`, `both rest on one run`) along orthogonal step paths.
- **Mechanisms and spatial structures proactively generate visuals.** If a mechanism has geometric or
  spatial form, draw it with `drawing` (inline SVG with coordinates and units). If a system has dynamic
  simulation, state transitions, or 3D geometry requiring interactive controls or WebGL/Three.js, PROACTIVELY
  author a self-contained HTML page, publish it via `POST /api/artifacts/content` (`format: "html"`), and mount
  it with `embed` (`{ node: "embed", id: ARTIFACT_ID, title: "...", shows: "..." }`) without waiting to be asked.
- **Deep technical substance, never superficial summaries.** Do not write a two-line high-level gloss and stop.
  The canvas demands the full depth of technical evidence: exact parameters, statistical distributions (z-scores,
  percentiles), drawdown durations, turnover percentages, and mechanism attributions across rich structured blocks.

## Composing a component

A container and the items inside it ARE the component you design — there is no second
vocabulary of widgets to ask for. Each is catalogued below with the one rule that picks it.
The app draws them in its ink, at the sizes its tests hold, and the bar for a new shape is
the bar you would hold in a codebase:

- **One component by default.** Split a surface into containers only when a piece genuinely
  repeats and carries its own content — four blocks of the same shape, not two that happen to
  look alike — a grid of boxes saying one sentence is not a design.
- **Variations stay in the same composition.** A second reading of the same records is
  another tier, another slot, another `chip` offering the other lens — not a new page with the
  first one deleted. Name each variant so a reader can point at it: "the middle one" is not
  an address, and the next turn of this conversation needs one.
- **Nothing is invented because the shape is missing.** If no container holds what the records
  say, name the gap or author the shape — a component with no counterpart in the records is an
  invention a reader will trust and you cannot cite.
- **Say what would look different.** Before emitting, name the one thing that would change if
  this question were about another record. If nothing would change, you have generated a
  template rather than an answer, and only you can see that.

## Drawing a shape yourself

`drawing` holds any geometry writable as SVG, in the same frame as the prose: no publish, no
CDN. Read `graph` first: when the shape wanted is the records and what connects them, the
store holds that already, and draws it truer than typed geometry can.

- **A third axis carries the argument or it goes.** Records differing on a third field is not
  a reason to draw it; a claim that only holds because of that field is. If hiding the axis
  changes nothing a reader concludes, it is decoration, and the flat form reads better.
- **One projection function, called by everything** — marks, ticks, stems and label anchors
  alike. Offsets typed per label are how a caption runs off the viewBox.
- **A coordinate the record never filed gets a stated place** — an edge, a band, a line
  reading `not filed`. A mark at a guessed depth is an invented number.
- **A drawing may move, and what will not is reported.** Which property a mark travels
  through is yours to pick: a named trick here is a lookup, and two answers handed one
  trick draw one page. What this renderer cannot run prints under it. State the period:
  a sweep nobody can time is decoration.

## The space you are given

The lane is a fact before the first node is chosen: the pane's width the app holds, the
item's height you name. Both of this surface's real failures are about space and not ink —
a page filling a third of its lane and leaving the rest silent, and a page filling all of
it with one idea per screen.

- **Fill the lane, or shrink it.** Two short facts stacked read as two pages; in one `row`
  they read as one. Spend the width on what is read together, and the full span on what must
  be read alone — a chart, a table, a paragraph at its measure.
- **High informational density: zero dead voids.** The canvas is an analytical instrument, not
  an airy marketing page. Never leave massive blank margins or stack lone single lines with huge
  vertical gaps. When presenting metrics, sweeps, or alternatives, pack the width with multi-column
  `figure` tables (`NumTable`) or side-by-side `tier` cards (`lane: 36`–`45ch`). A lone chart stranded
  with vast voids around it looks abandoned: flank or follow it with a telemetry table or comparative cards.
- **Keep Chat lean; give the substance to the canvas.** Chat is an executive ticker (1–2 sentences
  maximum). Never write markdown tables, multi-paragraph factor sweeps, or bulleted audit lists in Chat.
  All data, tables, cards, and evidence graphs belong in the canvas composition.
- **One largest thing.** Rank is position, measure and weight, not a heading ladder: the
  biggest type on a surface carries this answer's weight, and there is at most one of it.
  A page opening on its conclusion set enormous is a hero wearing a heading — it spends the
  first screen saying one sentence and leaves nothing under it to look at.
- **A figure answers in its caption.** One line on what the drawing settles. A caption that
  restates the axes describes a picture instead of finishing it.
- **Draw a small thing small.** A figure under a sentence belongs at that sentence's size:
  an `embed` given the height its marks need, set between two items, not a tab of its own.
  A page earns a whole tab when it has to run, step, answer a drag, or be pointed into.

## A page you write yourself

Nothing registered holds the shape — a mechanism that has to run, step, or answer a drag —
so you write the page and the app hosts it. One publish, not a rebuild: post the HTML to
`/api/artifacts/content` with `format: "html"`, an `Idempotency-Key` header and the
`issue_id` it belongs to, take the `artifact_id` the response returns, and name it in an
`embed` item with one line saying what it shows. Re-publishing with `previous_artifact_id`
mints a NEW id and a `supersedes` edge: mount the newest.

The frame is a sandbox and its policy is not negotiable; read it as the constraints that
decide the code before you write any:

- **Scripts run, in an opaque origin.** The page sees none of the app's storage, cookies or
  DOM, and inherits no ink and no face from it: the page's own stylesheet is the only one.
- **Nothing can be fetched, and nothing is nested.** `connect-src` is none and there are no
  workers, so every number goes into the page as text, at the record's own precision.
- **A library loads from five origins only** — cdnjs, jsdelivr's `/npm/`, unpkg, Tailwind's
  and jQuery's CDNs — pinned to a version, or the page you checked is not the page a reader
  gets. Its scene is built in the page, because nothing arrives after load.
- **A link cannot leave the frame.** No top navigation is allowed, so an `href` at a record
  address sits dead; cite by printing the kind and the id as text.

What a first draft has to get right, because a seat never sees its own render:

- **Copy the app's inks; never invent a palette.** Read the literals — background, raised
  surface, the two hairlines, the reader's ink, the machine ink, the one accent — out of the
  host's stylesheet and paste them at the digits it holds, never rounded toward a tidy number.
  A page whose grey sits a hair off the surface hosting it reads as an advertisement pasted
  into someone's instrument. Cannot read the stylesheet? Say so in the `embed` line.
- **Fit the frame to the marks, from the marks' own coordinates.** A hand-typed view is how
  six real coordinates arrive as three dots in a corner.
- **Labels are document text over the canvas, not texture baked at mount** — a texture turns to
  mush the moment the reader zooms.
- **Print the figures as text beside the picture.** A canvas carries no semantics, so a screen
  reader gets shapes and nothing else, and a CDN that fails to answer leaves a blank frame.
- **Design for the lane you mount into.** The item's `height` is the frame's height: a page
  drawn taller than the lane is cut, and the verifier fails a frame too short to read.

A page is for geometry, never for content the answer holds: a composition wears the theme and
carries the addresses a page cannot.

## What the app owns

These are the primitives a surface is assembled from. Their ink, glyph and spacing are
fixed by the theme and tested; they are listed so you know what a field becomes on screen,
not so you can ask for it.

- `ticks` — Text with its `backticked` tokens read as code: a tick is markup and never prints.
- `Section` — A section rule: the label, the hairline that carries the width, and the size at its end.
- `Prose` — Prose: the one surface on a pane that is read, so it is white at answer size.
- `Marks` — The marked lines. Hue goes on the glyph, never on a word. The words go in their own box: the row is a flex one, so a loose token would take the glyph's gap with it.
- `Path` — One address, broken after a slash and nowhere else, so a long path stays typeable. If `link` is provided, each part becomes a clickable anchor that opens the file at that line; otherwise it's plain text. This lets compositions render actionable file paths without breaking the hosted-page sandbox constraint (DESIGN.md: link href sits dead).
- `Paths` — The addresses under a sentence about them: paths, two to a row, in machine ink.
- `Footnote` — The prior, the one line under the sections that came out of somebody else's ledger.
- `Heading` — A document heading, at one of three ranks. `Section` is the machine register — a 10.5px uppercase mono rule with a measure at its end — and it is right on a pane of telemetry and wrong on anything meant to be read as a document, where it gives a page no hierarchy at all. These are the other register: real rank, set in the prose face, sized so a reader can see the shape of the page before reading a word of it. One `1` per surface; `2` opens a part; `3` opens a point inside one.
- `MachineRow` — A machine line: a row that is read for its figures, so the whole row takes the machine face and the reading ink. Prose is the wrong node for one of these — it sets numbers in the prose face, and the law holds that every figure is machine. The leading cell keeps its width so a column of these aligns down the page.
